title: Sony Xperia 1 VIII Keeps the Headphone Jack. That's Not the Story.

components.text: Sony Xperia 1 VIII Keeps the Headphone Jack. That's Not the Story.
Sony's €1,499 flagship launched with a viral AI camera controversy that buried the hardware news.

Sony unveiled the Xperia 1 VIII on May 13, and somewhere between the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and the redesigned camera module, the company managed to create one of 2026's most talked-about phones for reasons it probably didn't intend. The hardware is impressive enough: a telephoto sensor roughly four times larger than the previous generation, a 3.5mm headphone jack, microSD card expansion, and a design overhaul that ditches the continuous optical zoom system Sony has used since the Xperia 1 IV. But none of that got much oxygen.

Instead, it was the AI Camera Assistant that went viral, and not in the way Sony's marketing team had hoped. Within days of launch, promotional images showcasing the feature sparked enough backlash online to overshadow the actual device specs. The phone became a lightning rod in conversations about AI in photography, authenticity, and whether Sony had misread the room on what camera enthusiasts actually want from a phone that costs €1,499.

The irony is that the Xperia 1 VIII is, on paper, exactly the kind of phone a vocal subset of Android users claim they want. It has a 6.5-inch LTPO OLED display at 120Hz, 12GB of RAM, up to 1TB of storage with microSD expansion, IP65 rating, wireless charging, and that endangered 3.5mm jack. The camera array moves to three 48MP sensors for the main and ultrawide, though the telephoto drops to 12MP with a fixed 2.9x optical zoom instead of the variable zoom of prior models. Sony is positioning this as a more practical trade-off, and the larger sensor should help in low light.

But here's the thing: Sony isn't bringing the Xperia 1 VIII to the United States. Again. The pattern that started after 2023 continues, which means anyone in North America interested in this phone will need to import it through third-party retailers. Pre-orders opened in Europe and select Asian markets, with shipments starting June 19. Sony is sweetening the deal with a free pair of WH-1000XM6 headphones, which retail around €350 to €400 on their own.

The Xperia 1 VIII comes in four colors under Sony's new "Ore" design language, which gives the phone a rough, stone-like texture. The square camera module sits in the top left corner, a departure from the minimal look of previous Xperia flagships. It's a bold move for a company that's historically leaned conservative on design, and whether it lands will depend on how people feel about holding actual stone texture for hours at a time.

Sony's challenge has never been building capable hardware. The Xperia 1 VIII is extremely capable. The challenge is convincing people to pay flagship prices for a phone they can't easily buy, can't easily get serviced, and that now comes with an AI feature controversy baked into its launch story. The headphone jack is great. The AI baggage might cost more than Sony planned.
